catalog_quote: [p. 20] The contrastiveness of length is illustrated in the minimal pairs in (33). Long vowels are written with two symbols (e.g., <aa>, not <a:>). Makhuwa does not have automatic penultimate lenghtening as in other Bantu languages, such as Makwe and Makonde. [p. 34] 2.2.2 Intonation. Makhuwa is clearly a tonal language, but it has some intonational features as well. These include the indication of continuation of speech, question intonation, and emphasis. ... In some Bantu languages, including some with a similar conjoint/disjoint distinction such as Makonde, Makwe, Zulu and Sotho, an automatic lengthening of the penultimate syllable occurs at the end of a phonological phrase, thus indicating the right boundary of that phrase. Unlike these languages, Makhuwa does not have this penultimate lengthening. [p. 242] In English, F-marking is realised phonologically as stress, and every F-mark…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Makhuwa (makh1264) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had one item, Philippson 1991 (Glottolog 38907), whose Glottolog record does link Makhuwa [vmw]. The author's full-text PDF (542 pp., text layer) was downloaded from the DDL-CNRS site (byte-identical to the copy already), saved with a Makua-pages excerpt, the Glottolog JSON and the theses.fr record under, and logged in there. Philippson treats Makua (group XIV, P31, documentation rated '+', data second-hand from Cheng & Kisseberth 1981 and Stucky 1979, Imitthupi dialect) as a 'langue purement accentuelle' in his pitch accent sense: disyllabic stems carry the H-docking mark either on the prefix or on the stem-initial syllable (two patterns; pp. 399, 440-441, 507-508), Esaaka -cvcv stems only on the penult (fn. p. 441); his Annexe criterion 10 (status of the penultimate) records no demarcative penultimate accent for Makua, unlike Makonde-Maraba or Tumbuka/Sena. This is a tone/pitch accent statement, not word stress, and it agrees with the first-hand source already held by the project, van der Wal 2009 (pp. 20, 34: no automatic penultimate lengthening; tonal language), re-read here and given as the best statement. No source read states a word-stress position for Makhuwa. nothing remains to acquire from the item list.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Makhuwa is described as a tonal language (morphologically assigned H tones with tone doubling; lexical tone contrasts marginal per Kisseberth 2003). The only statements about stress-like prominence are negative: the language lacks the automatic phrase-penultimate lengthening typical of neighbouring Bantu languages, vowel length is lexically contrastive, and focus is not marked by stress. No source opened states a position for word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final long vowels occur only in ideophones or under emphasis; under emphasis the last syllable of a phrase 'can sometimes be lengthened' with a HL pattern (p. 34-35). Phrase-final position blocks tone doubling (Final Lowering / Long Fall).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the phonological phrase / sentence (penultimate lengthening as a phrase-boundary cue) rather than the word; van der Wal's data are Makhuwa-Enahara (Ilha de Moçambique, Nampula). Kisseberth 2003 (Ruvuma dialects) and Cheng & Kisseberth 1979-81 (Ikorovere) describe tone only.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement describes Makhuwa-Enahara, the variety of Ilha de Moçambique (Glottolog dialect 'Enaharra', enah1238, under makh1264). Kisseberth 2003 and Cheng & Kisseberth 1979-81 describe the Ruvuma dialects Ikorovere and Imitthupi of southern Tanzania (Glottolog may file these under Makhuwa-Meetto rather than makh1264); Sacramento 1906 is coastal Mozambican 'macúa' of unspecified dialect. All sources agree Makhuwa is tonal.

new_statements.reading: Makhuwa has no word-level stress statement in the first-hand literature: it is a tone language (mora-based H tones) with no automatic penultimate lengthening, i.e. no demarcative penultimate stress of the kind found in Makonde, Makwe, Zulu or Sotho. Philippson 1991 (the only works with stress in the title; second-hand, Imitthupi dialect) corroborates from the tonological side: Makua is a 'langue purement accentuelle' in his pitch accent sense (H docks on prefix or stem-initial; two patterns), and his Annexe criterion 10 (status of the penultimate) lists no demarcative penultimate accent for Makua (pp. 399, 440-441, 507-508). If the language is ever added to the catalog, the classification would be 'no word stress / tone (pitch accent)'; no source read gives a fixed stress position.

sources.citation: Kisseberth, Charles. 2003. Makhuwa (P30). In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds), The Bantu Languages, 546-565. London: Routledge.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 3 'Makhuwa phonology' (pp. 548-555: 3.1 vowels, 3.2 consonants, 3.3 vowel sequences, 3.4 tone). The word 'stress' does not occur in the chapter. Tone: 'There is no variety of Makhuwa known to us where there is anything resembling a fully articulated system of lexical tone contrasts'; H tone assigned morphologically; tone doubling blocked phrase-finally and on the second mora of a bimoraic phrase-penult syllable (Ruvuma dialects Ikorovere/Imitthupi). Silent on stress.
